scenes.narration: There's a price on this page that exists only to make you pick a different one.
scenes.visual: price-box, price-box, price-box — drawn in order, pen only

scenes.narration: It isn't there to be bought. It's there to be rejected.
scenes.visual: price-box, x-mark, question-mark — drawn in order, pen only

scenes.narration: Once you can see it, you can't stop seeing it. It's in almost every pricing page you've ever looked at.
scenes.visual: price-tag, grid, eye — drawn in order, pen only

scenes.narration: In two thousand eight, the behavioural economist Dan Ariely found a subscription offer from The Economist and thought it looked like a mistake.
scenes.visual: person, price-box, question-mark — drawn in order, pen only

scenes.narration: Three options. Web only, fifty-nine dollars. Print only, one hundred and twenty-five.
scenes.visual: price-box, price-box, coin — drawn in order, pen only

scenes.narration: Print and web — also one hundred and twenty-five dollars. Read that again.
scenes.visual: price-box, price-box, price-box, question-mark — drawn in order, pen only

scenes.narration: Print alone cost exactly the same as print plus web. Nobody would choose print alone. It's strictly worse for the identical price.
scenes.visual: price-box, x-mark, scale — drawn in order, pen only

scenes.narration: So Ariely ran it on a hundred students. Sixteen chose web only. Zero chose print only. Eighty-four chose the combo.
scenes.visual: bar-chart, person, checkmark — drawn in order, pen only

scenes.narration: Then he deleted the useless option and ran it again on a fresh hundred.
scenes.visual: price-box, x-mark, person, bar-chart — drawn in order, pen only

scenes.narration: Logically, nothing should change. Nobody wanted it. Removing it should just leave the same two choices and the same split.
scenes.visual: price-box, price-box, question-mark — drawn in order, pen only

scenes.narration: The result flipped. Without the decoy, sixty-eight chose web only and just thirty-two chose the combo.
scenes.visual: bar-chart, arrow-down, arrow-up — drawn in order, pen only

scenes.narration: The expensive option lost more than half its buyers — because a product nobody bought stopped standing next to it.
scenes.visual: bar-chart, price-box, x-mark, arrow-down — drawn in order, pen only

scenes.narration: Because you are very bad at judging what something is worth, and very good at judging which of two things is better.
scenes.visual: brain, scale, question-mark — drawn in order, pen only

scenes.narration: Ask someone what a hundred and twenty-five dollars of journalism is worth and they have no idea. There's no internal price list.
scenes.visual: coin, question-mark, brain — drawn in order, pen only

scenes.narration: But put print-only next to print-plus-web and the comparison is trivial: same money, more stuff. Obviously better.
scenes.visual: price-box, price-box, checkmark, arrow-up — drawn in order, pen only

scenes.narration: That comparison feels like a judgement about value. It isn't. It's a judgement about those two options.
scenes.visual: scale, price-box, price-box, x-mark — drawn in order, pen only

scenes.narration: And someone chose which two options you'd be comparing.
scenes.visual: person, price-box, price-box, grid — drawn in order, pen only

scenes.narration: The recipe is precise. You need a target — the thing you want sold.
scenes.visual: price-box, spotlight, checkmark — drawn in order, pen only

scenes.narration: Then you add a decoy that is clearly worse than the target, but not clearly worse than the third option.
scenes.visual: price-box, price-box, arrow-down — drawn in order, pen only

scenes.narration: The decoy's whole job is to be dominated by exactly one option.
scenes.visual: price-box, spotlight, arrow-up, price-box — drawn in order, pen only

scenes.narration: It makes the target look like a win, and a win is much easier to choose than a value judgement.
scenes.visual: checkmark, scale, brain, spotlight — drawn in order, pen only

scenes.narration: Popcorn sizes work this way. Phone storage tiers work this way.
scenes.visual: price-box, phone, grid — drawn in order, pen only

scenes.narration: So does almost every three-tier software page where the middle plan is mysteriously the best deal.
scenes.visual: price-box, price-box, price-box, spotlight — drawn in order, pen only

scenes.narration: Worth being careful here. A three-tier pricing page is not automatically a trick.
scenes.visual: price-box, checkmark, x-mark — drawn in order, pen only

scenes.narration: Sometimes the middle plan genuinely is the best fit for most people, and saying so is helpful, not manipulative.
scenes.visual: price-box, checkmark, person, scale — drawn in order, pen only

scenes.narration: And the effect is smaller in the wild than in the lab. Real buyers have budgets, brand loyalty, and a habit of leaving the page entirely.
scenes.visual: bar-chart, person, exit-door, coin — drawn in order, pen only

scenes.narration: The Economist study is a clean demonstration of a real mechanism — not a promise that it works on everyone, every time.
scenes.visual: bar-chart, question-mark, scale — drawn in order, pen only

scenes.narration: The defence is almost annoyingly simple, because the effect only works while all the options sit next to each other.
scenes.visual: price-box, price-box, price-box, eye — drawn in order, pen only

scenes.narration: Before you look at the tiers, decide what you actually need. Write the number down if you have to. Then look.
scenes.visual: coin, checkmark, price-tag — drawn in order, pen only

scenes.narration: The decoy can only move you if you arrive without a position, because it works by supplying one.
scenes.visual: price-box, arrow-up, x-mark, brain — drawn in order, pen only

scenes.narration: And when one option is transparently worse than another at the same price, that's not a bad deal you're being offered. That's a signpost.
scenes.visual: price-box, signpost, arrow-up — drawn in order, pen only

scenes.narration: Pointing at the option someone would like you to take. You're not being fooled about value. You're being handed a comparison, and comparisons are the one thing your brain never refuses.
scenes.visual: signpost, price-box, price-box, scale, brain, bar-chart — drawn in order, pen only
